## Hematology

- Laboratory tests to know
- Anemias

- Platelet disorders
- $ Immune thrombocytopenia purpura (ITP)
- White blood cell interpretation

## NOTES

## QUESTION #1

Which of the following measures are required to diagnose a patient with anemia?

1. Both low hemoglobin and hematocrit
2. Hemoglobin, hematocrit, and red blood cells, all must be low
3. Both low hemoglobin and mean corpuscular volume
4. Either low hemoglobin, hematocrit, or red blood cells

## ANEMIA

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

- Reduction in at least one RBC measure
- $ RBC count
- $ Hemoglobin
- $ Hematocrit

## Anemia Is NEVER Normal!

<!-- image -->

Always suspect that something is going on with the patient!

## Normal Doesn't Always Mean Normal

A perimenopausal patient experiences shortness of breath and fatigue following a very heavy menstrual cycle.

| Hgb Level             | Pre-cycle Hgb   | Post-cycle Hgb   |
|-----------------------|-----------------|------------------|
| Normal 12.1-15.2 g/dL | 14.6 g/dL       | 12.5 g/dL        |

## Anemia Classification

Every anemia in the world is categorized by describing the size and color of RBCs \_\_\_\_\_\_ cytic (Size) \_\_\_\_\_\_ chromic (Color)

Joshua Lanclos/APEA

<!-- image -->

## How Do You Know the Size of RBCs?

- Look at the MCV value
- $ MCV = Mean Corpuscular Volume
- $ \_\_\_\_\_\_-cytic

| MCV Value   | Cell Size   | Name       |
|-------------|-------------|------------|
| Low         | Too small   | Microcytic |
| Normal      | Normal      | Normocytic |
| High        | Too big     | Macrocytic |

"cytic" refers to the cell

## MCV Value

<!-- image -->

## How Do You Know the Color of RBCs?

- Look at the MCH value
- $ MCH = Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin
- $ \_\_\_\_\_\_-chromic

| MCH Value   | Cell Color   | Name         |
|-------------|--------------|--------------|
| Low         | Too pale     | Hypochromic  |
| Normal      | Just right   | Normochromic |
| High        | Too dark     | Hyperchromic |

"chromic" means color

## Reticulocytes

- Reticulocyte: immature RBC
- Reticulocyte count: normally 0-2.5% for adults
- $ Indicates the bone marrow's ability to produce RBCs

## QUESTION #2

What is the most common reason that the bone marrow would make small RBCs?

1. Low iron
2. Low GFR
3. Low folate
4. Alcohol use disorder

## Iron Panel

## Serum iron:

- Iron in the circulation

## Serum ferritin:

- Iron in storage

## Total iron-binding capacity:

- How much iron can be moved to storage
- Iron's "chance" of finding a binding site!

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Another Way to Think About TIBC

Egg count is high.

Capacity is low.

Iron count is high.

<!-- image -->

TIBC is low.

## Peripheral Smear

- A visual description of blood cells
- Consider ordering a peripheral smear when a patient presents with anemia.

## Microcytic Anemias

Common causes

1. Iron-deficiency anemia
2. Thalassemia

Less common causes

1. Anemia of chronic disease (<20%)
2. Sideroblastic anemia
3. Lead toxicity ➔ Presents just like IDA

## Iron-Deficiency Anemia (IDA)

- Microcytic, hypochromic anemia
- Causes
- $ Blood loss: most common (gynecologic or GI)
- $ Iron deficit
- Low iron intake
- Poor absorption
- Pregnancy (raises iron needs)

Egg count is low. Capacity is high.

<!-- image -->

Iron count is low. TIBC is high.

## QUESTION #3

Which symptom would be unexpected in a young adult patient who has irondeficiency anemia?

1. Brittle fingernails
2. Fatigue
3. Muscle cramps
4. Exercise intolerance

## Iron-Deficiency Anemia: Clinical Presentation

- Usually asymptomatic until Hgb ≤10
- Presentation varies by age

| Age                 | Presentation                                              |
|---------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| Young, middle adult | Fatigue, weakness, HA, irritability, exercise intolerance |
| Older adult         | Exacerbation of comorbidities (angina, HF, dementia)      |

## NOTES Which Iron Is the Best Supplement to Prescribe?

Elemental iron replacement

- Old recommendation: 150-200 mg daily
- New recommendation: 15-20 mg daily

## Thalassemia

Genetic abnormality that impairs the formation of hemoglobin and leads to abnormal RBCs

- Microcytic, hypochromic cells
- Diagnostic test: hemoglobin electrophoresis

## Hemoglobin

Patho: abnormal hemoglobin molecule

<!-- image -->

"Target cells" (Nucleated RBCs on peripheral smear)

<!-- image -->

<!-- image -->

Resulting in hemolysis or impaired erythropoiesis

## Comparison of Thalassemia and Iron-Deficiency Anemia

| Thalassemia   |                | Iron-Deficient Anemia   |
|---------------|----------------|-------------------------|
|               | Hct, Hgb       |                         |
|               | MCV, MCH       |                         |
| Normal        | RDW            |                         |
| Normal        | Serum Fe       |                         |
| Normal        | TIBC           |                         |
| Normal        | Serum ferritin |                         |

## Anemia of Chronic Disease

- Also called "anemia of chronic inflammation"
- Short RBC lifespan
- $ RBCs live 60-90 days (normal 100-120 days)
- $ Normocytic, normochromic anemia (long-standing: may be microcytic, hypochromic anemia)
- Management: better control/treatment of underlying condition

## Anemia of Chronic Disease Etiologies

- Rheumatoid arthritis
- Morbid obesity
- Colon cancer
- Diabetes mellitus (uncontrolled)
- Congestive heart failure
- COPD
- Chronic kidney disease
- Autoimmune disease
- Chronic infection (HIV)

Take a good history!

## Common Macrocytic Anemias

<!-- image -->

- They work together to form RBC, WBC, and platelets.
- Important in making DNA and RNA!
- Deficiencies in BOTH cause megaloblastic anemia!

## B12/Folate Deficiency

- Classic presentation
- $ Asymptomatic
- $ Unexplained neurologic symptoms (severe B12 deficiency):
- Cognitive changes
- Neuropathy
- Glossitis

## Etiology of B12 and Folate Deficiencies

Macrocytic

| Mechanism                | B12 Deficiency Causes                                                                                                     | Folate Deficiency Causes                                                                                                  |
|--------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Decreased dietary intake | Alcohol misuse, severely restricted diet, malnourishment                                                                  | Alcohol misuse, severely restricted diet, malnourishment                                                                  |
| Impaired absorption      | Pernicious anemia (PA), colchicine use                                                                                    | Hereditary folate malabsorption                                                                                           |
|                          | Alterations of GI tract: gastrectomy, ileitis, diverticulosis, sprue, celiac, Crohn disease, bariatric surgery, H. pylori | Alterations of GI tract: gastrectomy, ileitis, diverticulosis, sprue, celiac, Crohn disease, bariatric surgery, H. pylori |
| Impaired metabolism      | H2 blockers, metformin, PPI, GLP-1                                                                                        | Antiseizure drugs, triamterene, TMP- SMX, metformin, methotrexate                                                         |
| Increased needs          | Pregnancy, lactation, hemodialysis, cancer, hyperthyroidism                                                               | Pregnancy, lactation, hemodialysis, cancer, hyperthyroidism                                                               |

Large Red Blood Cell

<!-- image -->

## Vitamin B12 Management

## Symptomatic

- Vitamin B12 IM until symptoms resolved
- Repeat CBC at 2-3 weeks: increased retic count

## Asymptomatic

- Vitamin B12 IM, SQ, or PO until deficiency corrected
- CBC and vitamin B12 level in 4-8 weeks, then 6 months, then annual

TIP: Therapy duration and route depend on the cause.

## Folate Deficiency Management

- Folate: occurs naturally, RDA 200 mcg
- Folic acid: synthetic
- Oral folic acid
- $ 1-5 mg/d for 1-4 months if cause is reversible
- $ Indefinitely if chronic: (e.g., sickle cell, hemolytic anemias, methotrexate use)

## Warning!

Do not administer folic acid without first checking for vitamin B12 deficiency!

## NOTES

## NOTES Thrombocytopenia

- Decrease in platelet count (<150,000)
- $ Petechiae, purpura, and bleeding issues are far more likely with lower counts (<50,000)
- $ Platelets only cell affected, or there can be alterations in WBCs, RBCs

## Etiology of Thrombocytopenia

- Remainder of CBC normal
- $ Immune thrombocytopenia purpura ("idiopathic")
- $ Resolved viral/bacterial infection (triggered)
+ Leukocytosis
- Infection
- Inflammation
- Malignancy

## Leukocytes

WBCs (Leukocytes)

<!-- image -->

## WBC Differential

| Cell Type          | Function                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|--------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Neutrophils 40-60% | · First responders (soldiers), phagocytic · Main cells in purulent drainage · A.K.A. "NPs": neutrophils, polys, segs                                                                             |
| Lymphocytes 20-40% | · B cells (plasma cells): produce antibodies (e.g., IgM, IgE) · T cells: attack & kill antigens (invaders) & create a mugshot (memory) of the antigen                                            |
| Monocytes 2-8%     | · Dendritic cells: collect & identify antigen, sound the alarm to alert other fighter cells · Macrophages: ingest, kill, and remove invaders (increase in number after more than about 24 hours) |
| Eosinophils 1-4%   | · Allergies, asthma, drug reactions · Parasitic infections                                                                                                                                       |
| Basophils 0.5-1%   | · Nonspecific immunity; release histamine & heparin · Only recognize new/unfamiliar pathogens                                                                                                    |

## NOTES White Blood Cell Count

| Drugs              | · Epinephrine · Allopurinol · Aspirin · Heparin · Corticosteroids · Triamterene                                                                         | · Antibiotics (beta lactams) · Antiseizure medications · Chemotherapy drugs · Diuretics · Sulfa drugs                           |
